claim: Proteolysis of transmembrane receptors is a critical cellular communication mechanism dysregulated in disease.
source: Proteolysis of transmembrane receptors is a critical cellular communication mechanism dysregulated in disease, yet decoding proteolytic regulation mechanisms of hundreds of shed receptors is hindered by difficulties controlling stimuli and unknown fates of cleavage products.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of proteolysis in cellular communication and disease, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Decoding proteolytic regulation mechanisms of hundreds of shed receptors is hindered by difficulties controlling stimuli and unknown fates of cleavage products.
source: Proteolysis of transmembrane receptors is a critical cellular communication mechanism dysregulated in disease, yet decoding proteolytic regulation mechanisms of hundreds of shed receptors is hindered by difficulties controlling stimuli and unknown fates of cleavage products.
evidence: This statement describes a challenge in the field based on the authors' assessment of current research limitations.

claim: Notch proteolytic regulation involves intercellular forces that drive exposure of a cryptic protease site within a juxtamembrane proteolytic switch domain to activate transcriptional programs.
source: Notch proteolytic regulation is a notable exception, where intercellular forces drive exposure of a cryptic protease site within a juxtamembrane proteolytic switch domain to activate transcriptional programs.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about Notch signaling mechanisms.

claim: SNAPS exploits the modularity and unequivocal input/response of Notch proteolysis to screen surface receptors for putative proteolytic switches.
source: We created a Synthetic Notch Assay for Proteolytic Switches (SNAPS) that exploits the modularity and unequivocal input/response of Notch proteolysis to screen surface receptors for other putative proteolytic switches.
evidence: This describes the design and purpose of the SNAPS assay developed in this study.

claim: Several new proteolytic switches were identified among receptors with structural homology to Notch.
source: We identify several new proteolytic switches among receptors with structural homology to Notch.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SNAPS can detect shedding in chimeras of diverse cell surface receptors.
source: We demonstrate SNAPS can detect shedding in chimeras of diverse cell surface receptors, leading to new, testable hypotheses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing detection of shedding in various receptor chimeras.

claim: SNAPS can be used to measure modulation of proteolysis by potential therapeutics.
source: Finally, we establish the assay can be used to measure modulation of proteolysis by potential therapeutics and offer new mechanistic insights into how DECMA-1 disrupts cell adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of Herceptin and DECMA-1 on proteolysis.

claim: DECMA-1 disrupts cell adhesion through a mechanism involving proteolysis.
source: Finally, we establish the assay can be used to measure modulation of proteolysis by potential therapeutics and offer new mechanistic insights into how DECMA-1 disrupts cell adhesion.
evidence: This is a new mechanistic insight supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Diverse adhesion receptors such as cadherins are cleaved at sites close to the extracellular side of the membrane by metalloproteinases.
source: Diverse adhesion receptors, such as cadherins, as well as receptors that respond to soluble factors, such as receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), have been shown to be cleaved at sites close to the extracellular side of the membrane by metalloproteinases such as 'A Disintegrin And Metalloproteinases' (ADAMs) and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) (Kessenbrock et al., 2010; McCawley and Matrisian, 2001; Miller et al., 2017; Seals and Courtneidge, 2003; White, 2003), resulting in ectodomain shedding.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Receptor tyrosine kinases are cleaved at sites close to the extracellular side of the membrane by metalloproteinases.
source: Diverse adhesion receptors, such as cadherins, as well as receptors that respond to soluble factors, such as receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), have been shown to be cleaved at sites close to the extracellular side of the membrane by metalloproteinases such as 'A Disintegrin And Metalloproteinases' (ADAMs) and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) (Kessenbrock et al., 2010; McCawley and Matrisian, 2001; Miller et al., 2017; Seals and Courtneidge, 2003; White, 2003), resulting in ectodomain shedding.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Ectodomain shedding is a prerequisite for further cleavage inside the membrane by the γ-secretase/presenilin protease complex in a process known as Regulated Intramembrane Proteolysis (RIP).
source: In many of these receptors, ectodomain shedding is a prerequisite for further cleavage inside the membrane by the γ-secretase/presenilin protease complex in a process known as Regulated Intramembrane Proteolysis (RIP) (Brown et al., 2000; Selkoe and Wolfe, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on RIP.

claim: The intracellular fragment of Notch translocates to the nucleus and acts as a transcriptional co-activator.
source: Proteolysis not only provides a mechanism to break cell-cell and cell-ECM contacts to modulate processes such as cell migration, but may also result in biologically-active fragments outside and inside of the cell, such as the intracellular fragment of Notch, which translocates to the nucleus and acts as a transcriptional co-activator (Bray, 2006; Struhl and Adachi, 1998; Struhl and Greenwald, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on Notch signaling.

claim: Dysregulated proteolysis contributes to disease pathogenesis by causing accumulation of pathogenic fragments such as the amyloid beta peptide implicated in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Dysregulated proteolysis contributes to disease pathogenesis, for example, by causing accumulation of pathogenic fragments such as the amyloid beta peptide implicated in Alzheimer's disease (Goate et al., 1991; Scheuner et al., 1996), or removing epitopes required for normal cell communication (Boutet et al., 2009; Groh et al., 2002; Kaiser et al., 2007; Waldhauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on Alzheimer's disease.

claim: Cancer cells evade the immune response by shedding MICA receptors.
source: For instance, cancer cells evade the immune response by shedding MICA receptors (Boutet et al., 2009; Groh et al., 2002; Kaiser et al., 2007; Waldhauer et al., 2008), which are normally deployed to the cell surface in response to cellular damage.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on MICA shedding in cancer.

claim: Many protease inhibitors have failed clinically due to significant off-target effects.
source: Many protease inhibitors have been developed but have failed clinically due to significant off-target effects (Dufour and Overall, 2013; Turk, 2006; Vandenbroucke and Libert, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on protease inhibitor failures.

claim: Trastuzumab (Herceptin) acts, in part, by blocking proteolysis of the receptor tyrosine kinase HER2.
source: Conversely, relatively few examples of modulating access to protease sites in specific receptors have been reported, despite the clinical success of the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab (Herceptin) that was found to act, in part, by blocking proteolysis of the receptor tyrosine kinase HER2 (Molina et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on Herceptin's mechanism of action.

claim: Modulatory antibodies targeting proteolysis of Notch receptors have been successfully developed.
source: Similarly, successful development of modulatory antibodies targeting proteolysis of Notch (Agnusdei et al., 2014; Aste-Amézaga et al., 2010; Falk et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tiyanont et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010) and MICA (Ferrari de Andrade et al., 2018) receptors have recently been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research on Notch-targeting antibodies.

claim: Modulatory antibodies targeting proteolysis of MICA receptors have been successfully developed.
source: Similarly, successful development of modulatory antibodies targeting proteolysis of Notch (Agnusdei et al., 2014; Aste-Amézaga et al., 2010; Falk et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tiyanont et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010) and MICA (Ferrari de Andrade et al., 2018) receptors have recently been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on MICA-targeting antibodies.

claim: 8% of the annotated human transmembrane proteins are predicted to be shed from the surface.
source: However, although 8% of the annotated human transmembrane proteins are predicted to be shed from the surface (Tien et al., 2017), mechanisms of proteolytic regulation that inform development of specific modulators have remained elusive.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous computational study.

claim: Von Willebrand factor (VWF) is cleaved in its A2 domain in response to shear stress in the bloodstream, which regulates blood clotting.
source: For example, the secreted von Willebrand factor (VWF) is cleaved in its A2 domain in response to shear stress in the bloodstream, which regulates blood clotting (Dong et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on VWF cleavage.

claim: Transmembrane Notch receptors control exposure of a cryptic protease recognition site via the conformation of a juxtamembrane domain called the Negative Regulatory Region (NRR).
source: Transmembrane Notch receptors also control exposure of a cryptic protease recognition site via the conformation of a juxtamembrane domain called the Negative Regulatory Region (NRR) (Gordon et al., 2015; Gordon et al., 2009; Gordon et al., 2007; Sanchez-Irizarry et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2015) to trigger Notch signaling (Bray, 2006; Kopan and Ilagan, 2009) in response to ligand binding and subsequent endocytic forces (Gordon et al., 2015; Langridge and Struhl, 2017; Parks et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research on Notch NRR structure and function.

claim: Crystal structures of the NRR reveal that the ADAM10/17 protease site is housed in a Sea urchin Enterokinase Agrin-like (SEA-like) domain.
source: Crystal structures of the NRR (Gordon et al., 2009; Gordon et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2015) reveal that the ADAM10/17 protease site is housed in a Sea urchin Enterokinase Agrin-like (SEA-like), with high structural homology to canonical SEA domains of mucins (Macao et al., 2006; Maeda et al., 2004) but lacking the characteristic autoproteolytic site.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to crystal structure studies of the Notch NRR.

claim: Notch's SEA-like domain has high structural homology to canonical SEA domains of mucins but lacks the characteristic autoproteolytic site.
source: Crystal structures of the NRR (Gordon et al., 2009; Gordon et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2015) reveal that the ADAM10/17 protease site is housed in a Sea urchin Enterokinase Agrin-like (SEA-like), with high structural homology to canonical SEA domains of mucins (Macao et al., 2006; Maeda et al., 2004) but lacking the characteristic autoproteolytic site.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to structural studies comparing Notch SEA-like domain to mucin SEA domains.

claim: Canonical SEA domains of mucins contain a highly conserved αβ-sandwich ferredoxin fold despite low sequence conservation.
source: Canonical SEA domains of mucins contain a highly conserved αβ-sandwich ferredoxin fold despite low sequence conservation (Macao et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous structural research on mucin SEA domains.

claim: Notch's SEA-like domain was identified based on structural homology.
source: Notch's SEA-like domain was identified based on structural homology (Gordon et al., 2007) and a recent computational study identified several previously unidentified juxtramembrane domains predicted to exhibit an SEA-like fold (Pei and Grishin, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the original structural study identifying the Notch SEA-like domain.

claim: A recent computational study identified several previously unidentified juxtramembrane domains predicted to exhibit an SEA-like fold.
source: Notch's SEA-like domain was identified based on structural homology (Gordon et al., 2007) and a recent computational study identified several previously unidentified juxtramembrane domains predicted to exhibit an SEA-like fold (Pei and Grishin, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a computational study predicting SEA-like domains.

claim: The NRR normally exists in a proteolytic cleavage-resistant state in which the protease site is buried by interdomain interactions between the SEA-like and its neighboring domain.
source: The NRR normally exists in a proteolytic cleavage-resistant state in which the protease site is buried by interdomain interactions between the SEA-like and its neighboring domain but can be switched to a protease-sensitive state when it undergoes a conformational change upon binding a ligand on a neighboring cell and subsequent trans-endocytosis (Gordon et al., 2015; Parks et al., 2000; Sanchez-Irizarry et al., 2004) or if it harbors disease-related mutations that destabilize the domain (Gordon et al., 2009; Malecki et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on Notch NRR conformational states.

claim: The NRR can be switched to a protease-sensitive state when it undergoes a conformational change upon binding a ligand on a neighboring cell and subsequent trans-endocytosis.
source: The NRR normally exists in a proteolytic cleavage-resistant state in which the protease site is buried by interdomain interactions between the SEA-like and its neighboring domain but can be switched to a protease-sensitive state when it undergoes a conformational change upon binding a ligand on a neighboring cell and subsequent trans-endocytosis (Gordon et al., 2015; Parks et al., 2000; Sanchez-Irizarry et al., 2004) or if it harbors disease-related mutations that destabilize the domain (Gordon et al., 2009; Malecki et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on ligand-induced Notch activation.

claim: Disease-related mutations that destabilize the NRR domain can switch it to a protease-sensitive state.
source: The NRR normally exists in a proteolytic cleavage-resistant state in which the protease site is buried by interdomain interactions between the SEA-like and its neighboring domain but can be switched to a protease-sensitive state when it undergoes a conformational change upon binding a ligand on a neighboring cell and subsequent trans-endocytosis (Gordon et al., 2015; Parks et al., 2000; Sanchez-Irizarry et al., 2004) or if it harbors disease-related mutations that destabilize the domain (Gordon et al., 2009; Malecki et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on disease-causing Notch mutations.

claim: Notch's proteolytic switch has been exploited to develop conformation-specific modulatory antibodies.
source: Notch's proteolytic switch has been exploited to develop conformation-specific modulatory antibodies (Agnusdei et al., 2014; Aste-Amézaga et al., 2010; Falk et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tiyanont et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010) and harnessed for synthetic biology applications (Morsut et al., 2016) to turn on transcription in response to any desired cell-cell contact.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research on Notch-targeting antibodies.

claim: Notch's proteolytic switch has been harnessed for synthetic biology applications to turn on transcription in response to any desired cell-cell contact.
source: Notch's proteolytic switch has been exploited to develop conformation-specific modulatory antibodies (Agnusdei et al., 2014; Aste-Amézaga et al., 2010; Falk et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Qiu et al., 2013; Tiyanont et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010) and harnessed for synthetic biology applications (Morsut et al., 2016) to turn on transcription in response to any desired cell-cell contact.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on synthetic Notch applications.

claim: Notch was engineered to respond to novel inputs and create custom responses.
source: For example, Notch was engineered to respond to novel inputs and create custom responses (Roybal et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on engineered Notch receptors.

claim: The SynNotch system has been applied to CAR T-cell therapy to require dual antigen recognition for T-cell activation, increasing specificity.
source: This SynNotch system has been applied to CAR T-cell therapy to require dual antigen recognition for T-cell activation, increasing specificity.
evidence: This statement describes an application of SynNotch technology based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several cell-surface receptors harbor extracellular juxtamembrane domains with structural homology to Notch's proteolytic switch.
source: However, despite the knowledge that several cell-surface receptors harbor extracellular juxtamembrane domains with structural homology to Notch's proteolytic switch (Pei and Grishin, 2017) and that more than 100 receptors undergo a Notch-like proteolytic cascade (Brown et al., 2000; Selkoe and Wolfe, 2007), other membrane resident proteolytic switches have not been identified, in large part due to difficulties in studying proteolysis in most receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a computational study identifying structural homology.

claim: More than 100 receptors undergo a Notch-like proteolytic cascade.
source: However, despite the knowledge that several cell-surface receptors harbor extracellular juxtamembrane domains with structural homology to Notch's proteolytic switch (Pei and Grishin, 2017) and that more than 100 receptors undergo a Notch-like proteolytic cascade (Brown et al., 2000; Selkoe and Wolfe, 2007), other membrane resident proteolytic switches have not been identified, in large part due to difficulties in studying proteolysis in most receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on RIP substrates.

claim: The known VWF proteolytic switch domain could functionally substitute for the Notch NRR to facilitate Notch signaling in certain contexts in Drosophila.
source: A recent study showing that the known VWF proteolytic switch domain could functionally substitute for the Notch NRR to facilitate Notch signaling in certain contexts in Drosophila (Langridge and Struhl, 2017) inspired us to ask if we could exploit Notch signaling to discover new proteolytic switches.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study on VWF-Notch chimeras.

claim: SNAPS uses the native Notch ligand-binding interaction with DLL4 as the input and the Gal4 transcriptional response as the output.
source: SNAPS uses the native Notch ligand-binding interaction with DLL4 as the input and the Gal4 transcriptional response as the output (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the design of the SNAPS assay developed in this study, with reference to Figure 1A showing the schematic.

claim: Proteolysis regions of several receptors with structural homology to Notch can substitute for the Notch 'proteolytic switch' and facilitate signaling in response to cell contact.
source: Here, we find that proteolysis regions of several receptors with structural homology to Notch can substitute for the Notch 'proteolytic switch' and facilitate signaling in response to cell contact.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The assay can be used to detect shedding of diverse receptors such as RTKs and cadherins.
source: Moreover, the assay can be used to detect shedding of diverse receptors such as RTKs and cadherins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The assay can be used to screen modulators of proteolysis.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the assay can be used to screen modulators of proteolysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data with Herceptin and DECMA-1.

claim: Dystroglycan, Protocadherin-15 (PCDH15), and Cadherin-related protein 2 (CDHR2) could functionally substitute for Notch's NRR.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the ECM receptor dystroglycan and two protocadherins involved in intercellular adhesion, Protocadherin-15 (PCDH15) and Cadherin-related protein 2 (CDHR2), could functionally substitute for Notch's NRR (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dystroglycan, PCDH15, and CDHR2 chimeric receptors signaled robustly only in the presence of cells expressing DLL4.
source: These chimeric receptors signaled robustly only in the presence of cells expressing DLL4, and the signal was abrogated by both a global metalloproteinase inhibitor (BB-94) and an inhibitor of the subsequent intramembrane γ-secretase cleavage event (γ-secretase inhibitor; GSI).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing ligand-dependent signaling that is blocked by protease inhibitors.

claim: The signal from dystroglycan, PCDH15, and CDHR2 chimeric receptors was abrogated by both a global metalloproteinase inhibitor (BB-94) and a γ-secretase inhibitor (GSI).
source: These chimeric receptors signaled robustly only in the presence of cells expressing DLL4, and the signal was abrogated by both a global metalloproteinase inhibitor (BB-94) and an inhibitor of the subsequent intramembrane γ-secretase cleavage event (γ-secretase inhibitor; GSI).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing inhibitor effects on signaling.

claim: Trop2 and Cadherin-23 (CADH23) displayed a more moderate signaling activity in response to DLL4.
source: The putative cell adhesion molecules Trop2 and Cadherin-23 (CADH23) displayed a more moderate signaling activity in response to DLL4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing signaling levels of different chimeras.

claim: SEA/SEA-like domains without a structured neighboring domain, such as Mucin-1 (MUC1) and receptor tyrosine phosphatase-related islet antigen 2 (IA-2), exhibited a high level of proteolysis even in the absence of DLL4.
source: On the other hand, SEA/SEA-like domains without a structured neighboring domain, such as Mucin-1 (MUC1) and receptor tyrosine phosphatase-related islet antigen 2 (IA-2), exhibited a high level of proteolysis even in the absence of DLL4, suggesting they contain a constitutively exposed protease site in the context of this assay.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing constitutive signaling in these chimeras.

claim: MUC1 and IA-2 contain a constitutively exposed protease site in the context of the SNAPS assay.
source: On the other hand, SEA/SEA-like domains without a structured neighboring domain, such as Mucin-1 (MUC1) and receptor tyrosine phosphatase-related islet antigen 2 (IA-2), exhibited a high level of proteolysis even in the absence of DLL4, suggesting they contain a constitutively exposed protease site in the context of this assay.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed constitutive signaling behavior.

claim: Most chimeras lacking signaling activity also expressed at lower levels than Notch.
source: Most of the chimeras lacking signaling activity also expressed at lower levels than Notch, suggesting defects in expression or trafficking due to incorrect choice of domain termini.
evidence: This is supported by cell surface ELISA data comparing expression levels.

claim: IA-2 undergoes much higher rates of proteolysis than the other proteins studied.
source: We reasoned that high rates of shedding could result in apparently low cell-surface levels in the ELISA assay, so we repeated the ELISA assay with the addition of the metalloproteinase inhibitor BB-94. Indeed, IA-2 surface expression was substantially increased in the presence of BB-94 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), while surface levels of other receptors that exhibited constitutive signaling activity were not drastically affected by inhibitor treatment. This suggests that IA-2 undergoes much higher rates of proteolysis than the other proteins studied.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that BB-94 treatment substantially increased IA-2 surface expression.

claim: Protocadherin-15's N-terminal cadherin-like domain binds on the opposite face of the SEA-like domain than Notch's neighboring Lin12 Notch Repeat domain.
source: Although Notch and Protocadherin-15 exhibit similar conformational switch behavior in the signaling assay, Protocadherin-15's N-terminal cadherin-like domain binds on the opposite face of the SEA-like domain than Notch's neighboring Lin12 Notch Repeat domain, suggesting potentially different conformational switching propensities.
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Protocadherin-15 and Notch may have potentially different conformational switching propensities due to different modes of interdomain interaction.
source: Although Notch and Protocadherin-15 exhibit similar conformational switch behavior in the signaling assay, Protocadherin-15's N-terminal cadherin-like domain binds on the opposite face of the SEA-like domain than Notch's neighboring Lin12 Notch Repeat domain, suggesting potentially different conformational switching propensities.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural differences observed.

claim: Dystroglycan proteolysis by MMPs is enhanced in many pathogenic states.
source: Moreover, degrees of proteolysis observed correlated with alterations in cell migration phenotypes (Hayward and Gordon, 2018), an important finding given that dystroglycan proteolysis by MMPs is enhanced in many pathogenic states (Agrawal et al., 2006; Matsumura et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on dystroglycan proteolysis in disease.

claim: The chimera containing an intact dystroglycan proteolytic switch domain was substantially protected from MMP cleavage, showing only a two- to three-fold increase in signal when MMPs were added.
source: Indeed, while the chimera containing constitutively exposed protease sites displayed robust 30-fold activation in the SNAPS assay upon addition of MMPs, the chimera containing an intact proteolysis domain was substantially protected from MMP cleavage, showing only a two- to three-fold increase in signal when MMPs were added (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The chimera containing constitutively exposed dystroglycan protease sites displayed robust 30-fold activation in the SNAPS assay upon addition of MMPs.
source: Indeed, while the chimera containing constitutively exposed protease sites displayed robust 30-fold activation in the SNAPS assay upon addition of MMPs, the chimera containing an intact proteolysis domain was substantially protected from MMP cleavage, showing only a two- to three-fold increase in signal when MMPs were added (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The observed proteolytic switch-like behavior in the SNAPS assay is relevant to regulation of dystroglycan's cleavage by MMPs in its native context.
source: These results suggest that the observed proteolytic switch-like behavior is relevant to regulation of dystroglycan's cleavage by MMPs in its native context, and that this assay can be used to further test hypotheses about regulation and potential modulation of proteolysis in dystroglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MMP protection data and comparison to native dystroglycan studies.

claim: Proteolysis plays a major role in the function of cell surface receptors such as E-cadherin and receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs).
source: We next wanted to determine whether SNAPS could be used to detect membrane shedding of receptors that do not contain SEA-like domains. Proteolysis plays a major role in the function of cell surface receptors such as E-cadherin and receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) (Katayama et al., 1994; Merilahti et al., 2017; Okamoto et al., 1999), and dysregulation of proteolysis in these receptors is, for instance, linked to cancer pathogenesis (Arribas et al., 2011; Brouxhon et al., 2014; Katayama et al., 1994; Okamoto et al., 1999) and resistance to kinase inhibitor treatment (Colomer et al., 2000; Leitzel et al., 1995; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dysregulation of proteolysis in E-cadherin and RTKs is linked to cancer pathogenesis.
source: Proteolysis plays a major role in the function of cell surface receptors such as E-cadherin and receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) (Katayama et al., 1994; Merilahti et al., 2017; Okamoto et al., 1999), and dysregulation of proteolysis in these receptors is, for instance, linked to cancer pathogenesis (Arribas et al., 2011; Brouxhon et al., 2014; Katayama et al., 1994; Okamoto et al., 1999) and resistance to kinase inhibitor treatment (Colomer et al., 2000; Leitzel et al., 1995; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dysregulation of proteolysis in E-cadherin and RTKs is linked to resistance to kinase inhibitor treatment.
source: Proteolysis plays a major role in the function of cell surface receptors such as E-cadherin and receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) (Katayama et al., 1994; Merilahti et al., 2017; Okamoto et al., 1999), and dysregulation of proteolysis in these receptors is, for instance, linked to cancer pathogenesis (Arribas et al., 2011; Brouxhon et al., 2014; Katayama et al., 1994; Okamoto et al., 1999) and resistance to kinase inhibitor treatment (Colomer et al., 2000; Leitzel et al., 1995; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Herceptin blocks proteolysis of the RTK HER2 as part of its mechanism of action.
source: Moreover, therapeutic antibodies such as Herceptin (Molina et al., 2001) have been developed that block proteolysis of the RTK HER2 and similar proteolysis blocking antibodies have been developed for the MICA immune receptor to block cancer cells from evading the immune system (Ferrari de Andrade et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on Herceptin's mechanism.

claim: Proteolysis blocking antibodies have been developed for the MICA immune receptor to block cancer cells from evading the immune system.
source: Moreover, therapeutic antibodies such as Herceptin (Molina et al., 2001) have been developed that block proteolysis of the RTK HER2 and similar proteolysis blocking antibodies have been developed for the MICA immune receptor to block cancer cells from evading the immune system (Ferrari de Andrade et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on MICA-targeting antibodies.

claim: The protease sites responsible for receptor shedding in cadherins and RTKs map to a putatively unstructured region between a structured repeat and the transmembrane region.
source: Unlike the aforementioned receptors with putative protease sites housed in structured SEA/SEA-like domains, the protease sites responsible for receptor shedding in cadherins and RTKs map to a putatively unstructured region between a structured repeat and the transmembrane region (Cho et al., 2003; D'Huyvetter et al., 2017; Franklin et al., 2004; Harrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on cadherin and RTK cleavage sites.

claim: Significant basal proteolysis is observed in the Notch-HER2 chimera when co-cultured with MS5 cells alone, in contrast to Notch.
source: As expected, we observe significant basal proteolysis when the chimera is co-cultured with MS5 cells alone, in contrast to Notch (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Notch-HER2 chimera shows a reproducible enhancement of signaling when Notch ligands are present.
source: Interestingly, like Notch, we observe a reproducible enhancement of signaling when Notch ligands are present that is observed in most RTKs tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Exposure of cryptic protease sites could contribute to proteolytic regulation in RTKs, perhaps by altering conformations of dimers.
source: The relevance of this enhanced proteolysis when exposed to forces of cell to cell contact will be interesting to probe in future studies, but suggests that exposure of cryptic protease sites could contribute to proteolytic regulation in these receptors, perhaps by altering conformations of dimers.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed ligand-enhanced proteolysis in RTK chimeras.

claim: Herceptin treatment causes reproducible and statistically significant decreases in proteolysis of HER2-chimera expressing cells compared to IgG control.
source: We observed reproducible and statistically significant decreases in proteolysis in cells treated with Herceptin as compared to the IgG control (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: Proteolysis of HER2 chimera was reduced up to 40% by Herceptin treatment.
source: Proteolysis was reduced up to 40%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data quantifying the effect of Herceptin.

claim: E-cadherin proteolysis not only breaks the intercellular adhesion but also generates a soluble ectodomain that can activate RTK signaling pathways.
source: E-cadherin forms homotypic dimers between cells to facilitate cell adhesion. Proteolysis not only breaks the intercellular adhesion but also generates a soluble ectodomain that can activate RTK signaling pathways and alters localization of beta-catenin, which binds to the E-cadherin intracellular tail, from the membrane to the nucleus (David and Rajasekaran, 2012; Maretzky et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on E-cadherin proteolysis effects.

claim: E-cadherin proteolysis alters localization of beta-catenin from the membrane to the nucleus.
source: Proteolysis not only breaks the intercellular adhesion but also generates a soluble ectodomain that can activate RTK signaling pathways and alters localization of beta-catenin, which binds to the E-cadherin intracellular tail, from the membrane to the nucleus (David and Rajasekaran, 2012; Maretzky et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on E-cadherin proteolysis effects.

claim: The observed 10-fold increase in basal signaling of the Notch-cadherin chimera over Notch was abrogated by treatment with protease inhibitors.
source: The observed 10-fold increase in basal signaling (co-culture with MS5 cells) over Notch was abrogated by treatment with protease inhibitors and when the linker containing putative ADAM10 sites was removed, suggesting that the signal is due to shedding. (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The signal from the Notch-cadherin chimera is due to shedding.
source: The observed 10-fold increase in basal signaling (co-culture with MS5 cells) over Notch was abrogated by treatment with protease inhibitors and when the linker containing putative ADAM10 sites was removed, suggesting that the signal is due to shedding. (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of protease inhibitors and deletion of cleavage sites.

claim: DECMA-1 is a function-blocking E-cadherin antibody known to break cell-cell contacts and reduce tumorigenesis in mice.
source: DECMA-1 is a function-blocking E-cadherin antibody known to break cell-cell contacts and reduce tumorigenesis in mice (Brouxhon et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on DECMA-1.

claim: DECMA-1 binds to E-cadherin at the interface of the last two cadherin repeats (EC4 and EC5) near the membrane.
source: However, its mechanism of breaking cell-adhesions has remained elusive; the antibody binds to E-cadherin at the interface of the last two cadherin repeats (EC4 and EC5) near the membrane, but the N-terminal repeats EC1 and EC2 are responsible for the homotypic interactions presumed to be disrupted by the antibody.
evidence: This statement describes the known binding site of DECMA-1 based on established knowledge.

claim: When cells are treated with DECMA-1, a dose-dependent increase in the basal level of signaling is observed, in comparison to control antibody.
source: When the cells are treated with DECMA-1, we observe a dose-dependent increase in the basal level of signaling, in comparison to control antibody, almost to the level of ligand induced signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The apparent EC50 of DECMA-1 measured by the assay is ~0.8 μg/mL.
source: The apparent EC50 of DECMA-1 measured by the assay is ~0.8 μg/mL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mechanism of DECMA-1 breaking adhesive contacts could, in part, be due to increased shedding of the receptor from the membrane.
source: These data suggest that the mechanism of DECMA-1 breaking adhesive contacts could, in part, be due to increased shedding of the receptor from the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in proteolysis upon DECMA-1 treatment.

claim: E-cadherin is known to be cleaved by at least three enzymes.
source: E-cadherin is known to be cleaved by at least three enzymes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about E-cadherin proteolysis, illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: E-cadherin is first cleaved by ectodomain shedding by ADAM10 to form CTF1, which then makes the molecule a substrate for intramembrane cleavage by gamma-secretase to form CTF2.
source: The first is ectodomain shedding by ADAM10 to form CTF1, which then makes the molecule a substrate for intramembrane cleavage by gamma-secretase to form CTF2.
evidence: This statement describes the known proteolytic cascade for E-cadherin based on established knowledge.

claim: The intracellular domain of E-cadherin is known to be cleaved by Caspase-3 to generate CTF3, and this cleavage is enhanced in apoptotic cells.
source: Finally, the intracellular domain of E-cadherin is known to be cleaved by Caspase-3 to generate CTF3, and this cleavage is enhanced in apoptotic cells.
evidence: This statement describes known E-cadherin cleavage by caspase-3 based on established knowledge.

claim: A species at 37 kDa observed in all conditions has been previously assigned as CTF1.
source: We observe a species at 37 kDa in all conditions (Figure 4E), which has been previously assigned as CTF1 (Ferber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E and a citation to previous research.

claim: When cells are treated with gamma-secretase inhibitors, the intensity of CTF1 increases.
source: When cells are treated with gamma-secretase inhibitors, the intensity of CTF1 increases, further confirming the assignment of this band as CTF1 (Ferber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous research.

claim: A lower molecular weight species of ~28 kDa appears when cells are treated with DECMA-1.
source: Strikingly, a lower molecular weight species of ~28 kDa appears when cells are treated with DECMA-1, consistent with DECMA-1 enhancing proteolysis of E-cadherin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the western blot.

claim: The appearance of a ~28 kDa species when cells are treated with DECMA-1 is consistent with DECMA-1 enhancing proteolysis of E-cadherin.
source: Strikingly, a lower molecular weight species of ~28 kDa appears when cells are treated with DECMA-1, consistent with DECMA-1 enhancing proteolysis of E-cadherin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the appearance of a new cleavage product upon DECMA-1 treatment.

claim: When cells are treated with DECMA-1 and a caspase three inhibitor, the ~28 kDa band decreases about ~50%.
source: When cells are treated with DECMA-1 and a caspase three inhibitor, the band decreases about ~50% (quantification from two western blots shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), underscoring that it could be the caspase cleaved product.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intensity of the ~28 kDa band decreases 40% when cells are treated with gamma secretase inhibitors.
source: The intensity of the band also decreases 40% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) when cells are treated with gamma secretase inhibitors, along with a concomitant increase in CTF1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DECMA-1 increases proteolysis of endogenous E-cadherin in MCF7 cells.
source: Regardless of whether the fragment in CTF2 or CTF3, the result of DECMA-1 increasing proteolysis of endogenous E-cadherin in a relevant cancer cell line not only provides validation of using the SNAPS assay to study proteolysis in diverse receptors but also provides new mechanistic insight into how DECMA-1 functionally disrupts cell to cell adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the western blot analysis.

claim: Almost all of the receptors harboring SEA/SEA like domains in tandem with neighboring domains showed a similar switch-like behavior in the intercellular signaling assay.
source: We were struck by the fact that almost all of the receptors harboring SEA/SEA like domains in tandem with neighboring domains showed a similar switch-like behavior in the intercellular signaling assay, despite having neighboring domains with very different predicted structural characteristics.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data from the SNAPS assay.

claim: The different modes of interdomain interactions in SEA-like domain containing receptors suggest that the proteolytic switches may have different propensities to 'switch on'.
source: These different modes of interdomain interactions suggest that the proteolytic switches may have different propensities to 'switch on' as well as potentially different requirements for direction of applied force.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural comparisons.

claim: The different modes of interdomain interactions in SEA-like domain containing receptors suggest potentially different requirements for direction of applied force.
source: These different modes of interdomain interactions suggest that the proteolytic switches may have different propensities to 'switch on' as well as potentially different requirements for direction of applied force.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural comparisons.

claim: The structural differences in proteolytic switches may be a consequence of cellular context, for example receptor involved in intercellular versus ECM interactions.
source: Future studies probing comparative anatomy of putative proteolytic switches may reveal whether the structural differences are a consequence of cellular context; for example receptor involved in intercellular versus ECM interactions.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential reasons for structural differences.

claim: A switch that requires more 'force' to switch on could be used to distinguish an epitope that is presented on a tumor with a stiff ECM compared to a normal cell.
source: For example, in CAR-T applications, perhaps a switch that requires more 'force' to switch on could be used to distinguish an epitope that is presented on a tumor with a stiff ECM compared to a normal cell.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of different proteolytic switches.

claim: The smaller and structurally simpler design of the Cadherin-like neighboring domains of dystroglycan and protocadherin-15 might permit more facile trafficking and expression for certain applications.
source: Moreover, the smaller and structurally simpler design of the Cadherin-like neighboring domains of dystroglycan and protocadherin-15 might permit more facile trafficking and expression for certain applications.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential advantages of certain proteolytic switches.

claim: Constitutively proteolyzed MUC1 and IA2 exhibit much higher expression/rates of proteolysis and may provide opportunities for engineering more robust switches when paired with a neighboring domain.
source: Finally, constitutively proteolyzed MUC1 and IA2 exhibit much higher expression/rates of proteolysis and may provide opportunities for engineering more robust switches when paired with a neighboring domain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed high proteolysis rates of MUC1 and IA2.

claim: High levels of MMPs and thus dystroglycan cleavage have been observed in muscle biopsies of muscular dystrophy patients.
source: Moreover, high levels of MMPs and thus dystroglycan cleavage have been observed in muscle biopsies of muscular dystrophy patients (Matsumura et al., 2005), and treatment of muscular dystrophy mouse models with broad spectrum metalloprotease inhibitors has been shown to ameliorate symptoms in a muscular dystrophy mouse model (Kumar et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on dystroglycan cleavage in disease.

claim: Treatment of muscular dystrophy mouse models with broad spectrum metalloprotease inhibitors has been shown to ameliorate symptoms.
source: Moreover, high levels of MMPs and thus dystroglycan cleavage have been observed in muscle biopsies of muscular dystrophy patients (Matsumura et al., 2005), and treatment of muscular dystrophy mouse models with broad spectrum metalloprotease inhibitors has been shown to ameliorate symptoms in a muscular dystrophy mouse model (Kumar et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on MMP inhibitor treatment.

claim: The dystroglycan proteolytic switch might offer a receptor-specific therapeutic target in diseases where MMP cleavage is dysregulated.
source: The dystroglycan proteolytic switch might offer a receptor-specific therapeutic target in diseases where MMP cleavage is dysregulated.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: E-cadherin is involved in intercellular adhesions and transmission of mechanical stimuli.
source: Like Notch (Gordon et al., 2015; Langridge and Struhl, 2017; Parks et al., 2000), E-cadherin (Schwartz and DeSimone, 2008) and Protocadherin-15 are involved in intercellular adhesions and transmission of mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Protocadherin-15 is involved in sensing sound vibrations across stereocilia tip links in the process of hearing.
source: Protocadherin-15, for example, is involved in sensing sound vibrations across stereocilia tip links in the process of hearing (Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on Protocadherin-15 function.

claim: The ECM receptor CD44 is hypothesized to sense the stiffness of the ECM resulting in increased cell migration.
source: For example, the ECM receptor CD44 is hypothesized to sense the stiffness of the ECM resulting in increased cell migration (Kim and Kumar, 2014; Razinia et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on CD44 mechanosensing.

claim: The ECM receptor dystroglycan is thought to act as a shock absorber to protect the sarcolemma during muscle contraction.
source: Additionally, the ECM receptor dystroglycan is thought to act as a shock absorber to protect the sarcolemma during muscle contraction (Barresi and Campbell, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on dystroglycan function.

claim: The RTK AXL has been shown to be a rigidity sensor.
source: Finally, even receptors that do not reside at canonical force sensing structures of cells have been implicated in mechanosensing. The RTK AXL which binds to a secreted ligand Gas6 has been shown to be a rigidity sensor (Yang et al., 2016) and facilitate a decrease in cellular stiffness in lung cancer (Iida et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on AXL mechanosensing.

claim: AXL facilitates a decrease in cellular stiffness in lung cancer.
source: The RTK AXL which binds to a secreted ligand Gas6 has been shown to be a rigidity sensor (Yang et al., 2016) and facilitate a decrease in cellular stiffness in lung cancer (Iida et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research on AXL in cancer.

claim: Many receptors exhibit increased proteolysis in response to mechanical forces, suggesting that proteolysis may be a common mechanism used by cells to communicate mechanical stimuli.
source: Thus, our studies showing that many receptors exhibit increased proteolysis in response to mechanical forces suggest that proteolysis may be a common mechanism used by cells to communicate mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing ligand-enhanced proteolysis in multiple receptors.

claim: In the chimeric signaling assay, putative regions of proteolysis are evaluated in the context of artificial linkages at their N- and C-termini as well as potentially non-native stimuli and non-physiological presentation of proteases.
source: In the chimeric signaling assay, putative regions of proteolysis are evaluated in the context of artificial linkages at their N- and C-termini as well as potentially non-native stimuli and non-physiological presentation of proteases.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the SNAPS assay approach.

claim: The use of the Notch transmembrane domain in the chimeric receptors likely associates with the Notch membrane-tethered proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17.
source: The use of the Notch transmembrane domain in the chimeric receptors also introduces some caveats as the domain, together with membrane proteins such as tetraspanins (Zimmerman et al., 2016), likely associates with the Notch membrane-tethered proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of the Notch transmembrane domain and a citation.

source: Finally, the chimeric Notch signaling assay provides a stimulus for exposing protease sites involving a 2–5 pN force normal to the cell surface.
